RagShortTexts: Genoese crossbowmen paired heavy steel arbalests with pavises, dominating European.

Variants.Content: Genoese crossbowmen were Europe's most sought-after ranged professionals, and French, Sicilian, and Byzantine monarchs all hired them. They fought in pairs. One soldier planted a towering painted pavise shield in the ground to cover them, while the crossbowman wound a heavy composite arbalest and loosed a bolt that could pierce knightly mail at close range. The pavise and the crossbow worked together, because a man reloading behind a wall of wood was safe from the arrows of the enemy. Their skill made them the backbone of many armies, and their pay reflected it.

Organized into disciplined companies under civic podestàs, Genoese mercenaries demanded gold coin up front, and a lord who wanted their service paid for it before they took the field. On naval decks or at siege works, their suppressive volleys could decide an engagement across the Mediterranean.

Winding the cranequin ratchet draws the bowstring under immense tension, and your arms tremble before the cord clicks into the catch. When a square-headed steel quarrel snaps loose, it smashes through padded gambesons like dry firewood. Your pavisor must keep the shield steady, because one gust or one slip can leave you exposed.
